## plugin:small-business:shopify
This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

## Store Management
Once a store exists, this server provides tools for managing it:
- Products: search, create, update, bulk-update status, and organize into collections.
- Collections: search, create, update, and manage product groupings.
- Orders: list recent orders and get detailed order information.
- Customers: list and search customers.
- Inventory: check inventory levels and set quantities at specific locations.
- Analytics: run ShopifyQL queries for sales, order, and product performance data.
- Discounts: create percentage-based discount codes.

## GraphQL — General-Purpose Access
The Shopify Admin API exposes hundreds of resources. The built-in tools above are optimized shortcuts for common operations (with structured output and widgets), but they only cover a subset of the API.
When the user asks about a resource that has no dedicated built-in tool — such as gift cards, metafields, metaobjects, pages, blogs, markets, translations, publications, and many others — fulfill the request with the GraphQL Workflow below. NEVER tell the user that data is unavailable just because there is no built-in tool for it.

Decision logic:
1. If a built-in tool matches the request, prefer it (better UX).
2. If no built-in tool matches, run the GraphQL Workflow below. Do NOT open with graphql_query or graphql_mutation — the workflow starts at graphql_schema.

The electricity generation costs for PV battery systems vary in the analysis for Germany between 6.0 and 22.5 Cent pro kWh. By 2045, a further decline in electricity generation costs for new ground-mounted systems to 3.1 to 5.0 Cent pro Kilowattstunde is expected.

According to the Freiburg researchers, photovoltaic systems combined with battery storage are also now cheaper than conventional power plants.

Basierend auf meiner Websuche kann ich Ihnen umfassende Informationen zu Ihren Anfragen geben:

## Batteriegroßspeicher Deutschland: Erlöse 2025 (€/MW Jahr)

Das Erlöspotenzial lag 2025 bei rund 260.000 EUR pro MW und Jahr (2h-System, ISEA-Index) — real erreichen gut vermarktete Großspeicher typischerweise etwa 80 % davon.

### Erlösentwicklung nach Produkttyp:

**FCR (Primärregelleistung):**
FCR ist durch den Speicherzubau unter Druck (Potenzial 2025: rund 106.000 EUR/MW, fallend). Im Zwei-Stunden-System gingen die FCR-Erlöse um über 90 Prozent zurück und spielen im optimierten Fahrplan kaum noch eine Rolle.

**aFRR (Sekundärregelleistung):**
Der größte Einzeltopf ist inzwischen die aFRR-Kapazitätsvermarktung (Erlöspotenzial 2025: rund 146.000 EUR/MW, +39 % gegenüber 2024).

**Arbitrage:**
Laut ISEA Battery Revenue Index legten die Arbitrage-Erlöspotenziale 2025 um rund 17 Prozent zu, während einzelne Regelenergie-Segmente einbrachen.

## BGH Urteil zu Baukostenzuschuss für Speicher

Der Bundesgerichtshof (BGH) hat am 15.7.2025 (Az. EnVR 1/24) entschieden, dass die Erhebung eines nach dem Leistungspreismodell ermittelten Baukostenzuschusses (BKZ) für Batteriespeicher zulässig ist.

Zwar unterscheiden sich Batteriespeicher von anderen Letztverbrauchern dadurch, dass sie den aus dem Verteilernetz entnommenen Strom nicht verbrauchen, sondern zeitversetzt wieder einspeisen. Der nach dem örtlichen Leistungspreis berechnete Baukostenzuschuss wirkt bei Batteriespeichern stärker standortsteuernd als bei anderen Letztverbrauchern.

Die Entscheidung sorgt für einen Rückschlag für die Speicherbranche, bringt aber auch Rechtssicherheit für die Planung künftiger Speicherprojekte.

Institutional ground-mounted solar projects achieve 5 to 8 percent IRR per year with conservative, unlevered calculation. This is the typical range for realistic returns on Freiflächenanlage (ground-mounted) projects.

- PV ground-mounted systems with capacity under 1,000 kWp can receive a fixed feed-in tariff of 6.79 cents/kWh in 2025

29:  slug: "parkplatz-solarpflicht-bundeslaender",
42:    "Photovoltaik Pflicht Stellplätze",
56:    "Die Schwellen reichen von **mehr als 25 Stellplätzen (Niedersachsen)** bis **mehr als 70 Stellplätzen (Schleswig-Holstein)**. Meist müssen 30 bis 60 % der geeigneten Stellplatzfläche überdacht werden.",
69:          text: "**Eine Solarpflicht für neue Parkplätze gilt nach aktuellem Stand in Baden-Württemberg, Hamburg, Hessen, Niedersachsen, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Rheinland-Pfalz, im Saarland und in Schleswig-Holstein.** Sie greift jeweils erst ab einer Mindestzahl an Stellplätzen und in der Regel nur beim Neubau oder bei großen Erweiterungen, nicht für bestehende Parkplätze.",
73:          text: "Die [Parkplatz-Solarpflicht](/wissen/lexikon#parkplatz-solarpflicht) ist Landesrecht und steht mal in der Bauordnung, mal im Klimaschutz- oder Energiegesetz. Deshalb unterscheiden sich nicht nur die Schwellen, sondern auch die Details: Wer ist verpflichtet? Zählen Stellplätze für Wohnungen mit? Darf die Pflicht auf einem Dach statt über dem Parkplatz erfüllt werden? Die folgende Übersicht fasst das zusammen – für ein konkretes Bauvorhaben ersetzt sie nicht den Blick in den aktuellen Gesetzestext und die Abstimmung mit der Bauaufsicht.",
90:          text: "**Die Tabelle zeigt für jedes Land die Schwelle, den Stichtag, die Rechtsgrundlage und den geforderten Umfang.** Angaben „mehr als 35“ bedeuten: Die Pflicht beginnt ab dem 36. Stellplatz.",
97:            ["Baden-Württemberg", "ja", "mehr als 35 Stellplätze", "01.01.2022", "§ 23 KlimaG BW, PVPf-VO", "60 % der Eignungsfläche; Ersatz auf neuem Gebäude in der Nähe möglich"],
102:            ["Hamburg", "ja", "mehr als 35 neue Stellplätze (auch Erweiterung)", "01.01.2024", "§ 16a HmbKliSchG, PVUmsVO", "40 % der geeigneten Fläche; Ersatz auf Dächern desselben Grundstücks"],
103:            ["Hessen", "ja", "mehr als 50 (landeseigen: mehr als 35)", "Bauantrag nach 29.11.2023", "Hessisches Energiegesetz (HEG)", "Anlage über der Stellplatzfläche"],
106:            ["Nordrhein-Westfalen", "ja", "mehr als 35 notwendige Stellplätze eines Nichtwohngebäudes", "01.01.2022", "§ 48 Abs. 1a BauO NRW, SAN-VO NRW", "30 % der geeigneten Fläche; alternativ ein Laubbaum je 5 Stellplätze"],
107:            ["Rheinland-Pfalz", "ja", "ab 50 Stellplätzen (gewerblich, öffentlich)", "01.01.2023 (öffentlich 2024)", "Landessolargesetz (LSolarG)", "60 % der geeigneten Fläche; Ersatz in unmittelbarer Nähe"],
108:            ["Saarland", "ja", "ab 35 gewerblich genutzten Stellplätzen, öffentliche Parkplätze", "2025", "§§ 12a, 12b LBO Saarland", "60 % der geeigneten Fläche; Ersatz auf Dach desselben Grundstücks"],
111:            ["Schleswig-Holstein", "ja", "mehr als 70 Stellplätze (vorher mehr als 100)", "Novelle 2025, Übergangsjahr", "§ 25 EWKG", "Neubau und grundlegende Sanierung; geeignete Stellplatzfläche"],
120:          text: "Parkplätze, die unmittelbar an öffentlichen Straßen liegen, sind in mehreren Ländern ausgenommen. In Baden-Württemberg zählen nur Flächen, auf denen mindestens vier Stellplätze zusammenhängend für Pkw angeordnet sind; über Fahrgassen müssen keine Module stehen.",
136:            "**Hamburg:** Ausnahme u. a., wenn die Kosten der PV-Anlage 20 % der Baukosten der Stellplatzanlage übersteigen, bei nur vorübergehend genutzten Stellplätzen oder wenn kein Netzanschluss möglich ist.",
137:            "**Nordrhein-Westfalen:** Die SAN-VO nennt eine Amortisationszeit von über 25 Jahren als Grenze; Stellplätze direkt an öffentlichen Straßen sind ausgenommen. Alternativ kann ein Laubbaum je fünf Stellplätze gepflanzt werden.",
158:          text: `**Ein Solarcarport kostet je kWp deutlich mehr als ein Solarpark, rechnet sich aber, wenn der Strom im angrenzenden Gebäude verbraucht wird.** Wir rechnen mit ${fmt(CARPORT.capexProKwp.min)} bis ${fmt(CARPORT.capexProKwp.max)} €/kWp inklusive Stahlbau, Fundamenten und Entwässerung – gegenüber rund ${fmt(FREIFLAECHE.capexProKwp.mittel)} €/kWp bei Freiflächenanlagen. Je Stellplatz passen etwa ${fmt(CARPORT.kwpProStellplatz, 1)} kWp.`,
162:          caption: `Rechenbeispiel: Kundenparkplatz mit ${STELLPLAETZE} Stellplätzen, ${fmt(UEBERDACHT * 100)} % überdacht (West-/Mitteldeutschland)`,
165:            ["Überdachte Stellplätze", `${fmt(STELLPLAETZE * UEBERDACHT)}`, `${fmt(UEBERDACHT * 100)} % von ${STELLPLAETZE}`],
166:            ["Anlagenleistung", `${fmt(KWP, 1)} kWp`, `${fmt(CARPORT.kwpProStellplatz, 1)} kWp je Stellplatz`],
186:          text: "Stellplätze, Überdachungsgrad, Eigenverbrauch und Ladepunkte eingeben – mit Investition, Ertrag und Rendite.",
198:          text: "**Neben der Solarpflicht gilt bundesweit das Gebäude-Elektromobilitätsinfrastruktur-Gesetz (GEIG): Neue Nichtwohngebäude mit mehr als sechs Stellplätzen brauchen Leitungsinfrastruktur für mindestens jeden dritten Stellplatz und mindestens einen Ladepunkt (§ 7 GEIG).** Bestehende Nichtwohngebäude mit mehr als 20 Stellplätzen müssen seit dem 1. Januar 2025 mindestens einen Ladepunkt haben (§ 10 GEIG).",
235:            ["Pflicht prüfen", "Landesrecht, Stellplatzzahl, Nutzung (gewerblich, öffentlich, Wohnen) und Stichtag des Bauantrags klären."],
253:      q: "Ab wie vielen Stellplätzen gilt die Solarpflicht für Parkplätze?",
254:      a: "Das hängt vom Bundesland ab: in Niedersachsen ab mehr als 25 Stellplätzen, in Baden-Württemberg, Hamburg und NRW ab mehr als 35, im Saarland ab 35 gewerblich genutzten, in Hessen ab mehr als 50, in Rheinland-Pfalz ab 50 und in Schleswig-Holstein ab mehr als 70 Stellplätzen.",
266:      a: "Nein. § 32a BbgBO, der seit Juni 2024 für Parkplätze von Nichtwohngebäuden mit mehr als 35 Stellplätzen galt, wurde mit dem Vierten Gesetz zur Änderung der Brandenburgischen Bauordnung aufgehoben; die Neufassung gilt seit dem 30. Juni 2026.",
269:      q: "Wie viel kostet ein Solarcarport je Stellplatz?",
270:      a: `Bei rund ${fmt(CARPORT.kwpProStellplatz, 1)} kWp je Stellplatz und ${fmt(CARPORT.capexProKwp.min)} bis ${fmt(CARPORT.capexProKwp.max)} €/kWp ergeben sich etwa ${fmtEur(CARPORT.kwpProStellplatz * CARPORT.capexProKwp.min)} bis ${fmtEur(CARPORT.kwpProStellplatz * CARPORT.capexProKwp.max)} je überdachtem Stellplatz, ohne Ladepunkte und Netzverstärkung.`,

I've performed the web search for your query on § 118 Abs. 6 EnWG regarding network charge exemption for battery storage with commissioning until 2029 and a 20-year period.

Here are the key findings:

**Current Legal Regulation:**

§ 118 Abs. 6 EnWG guarantees newly constructed storage facilities that connect to the grid by August 3, 2029 with a 20-year exemption from network charges. This applies to battery storage systems commissioned between August 4, 2011 and August 4, 2029.

**Scope and Purpose:**

Battery storage systems are privileged in that they are exempt from network charges for the acquisition of energy to be stored for 20 years from commissioning. The privilege aims to avoid double charging and to promote investments.

**Recent Developments:**

In January 2026, the Bundesnetzagentur (German Federal Network Agency) proposed abolishing the privilege prematurely, before August 4, 2029. However, the verification of trust protection confirms that storage systems retain their 20-year exemption if they are commissioned by August 4, 2029.

**Definition of Commissioning:**

A power storage system is considered commissioned "upon its first power draw for test operation" (§ 118 Absatz 6 Satz 6 EnWG), meaning that the commercial commissioning date is not decisive.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

input.message:
## Report: ÖkoInvest investor, calculator, carport, storage and municipality pages

All 9 routes are built and return HTTP 200. I screenshotted each one at 1440 and 390 px and ran the calculators with interactions (switching the revenue model, chart hover and tooltip, "Kumuliert" toggle, table, toggles). There is no horizontal overflow at 390 px. The four logic files pass their Node self-tests (`node src/lib/rechner/<name>.js`). I have not committed anything.

### Routes and files
- **`/investoren`**: offer (6 cards), honest pipeline graphic (schematic, durations taken from `PHASEN.monateBisRtb`), phase model with price and risk per phase, interactive due-diligence checklist (24 items), 6-step platform process (Suchprofil → Matching → NDA → Datenraum → LOI → SPA/Closing), commission section with a worked example, search-profile form `typ="investor"` sending ticket size, phases, countries and technology as `daten`, FAQ. JSON-LD Service. Components in `src/components/Investoren/` (Phasenmodell, PipelineGrafik, DdCheckliste, InvestorAnfrage).
- **`/rechner/solarpark`**: project IRR and equity IRR, LCOE (nominal, discounted at WACC), NPV, payback, minimum DSCR. Cashflow chart over the full life (stacked bars: revenue / costs / debt service, plus an equity cashflow line) with a second "cumulative" view. 5×5 sensitivity matrix (capex × power price, switchable between project and equity IRR). Collapsible year-by-year table.
  - EEG is modelled as a floor under the market price, as in the German market-premium scheme.
  - The loan can optionally be capped at DSCR 1.15, the way banks size debt.
  - Adjustable life of 20–40 years. Results panel stays pinned on desktop.
  - Logic: `src/lib/rechner/solarpark.js`.
- **`/rechner/projektbewertung`**: price range per kWp and in total, risk level, value drivers and value reducers (grid status, cable distance, size, EEG/PPA, country), a "value staircase" chart, and a box linking to `/projektboerse/anbieten`. Logic: `src/lib/rechner/projektbewertung.js`.
- **`/solarcarport`**: inline SVG illustration plus three construction-type sketches, parking-lot solar-duty table for 8 German states with "Stand September 2026" and a caveat (kept consistent with the existing Ratgeber article), steel vs. wood, EV charging and GEIG, buy vs. contracting with live example figures, form `typ="carport"`, FAQ.
- **`/rechner/solarcarport`**: buy vs. contracting. The contracting price is derived from the contractor's full costs (annuity at WACC + O&M − surplus revenue, plus margin). Chart of cumulative advantage over 25 years. Logic: `src/lib/rechner/carport.js`.
- **`/grossspeicher`**: co-location vs. stand-alone, revenue streams with a schematic daily-profile SVG, example size (10 MW / 20 MWh) from `SPEICHER`, grid connection, BGH ruling of 15.07.2025 on construction-cost contributions (Baukostenzuschuss), § 118 (6) EnWG grid-fee exemption until 4 Aug 2029 (worded cautiously because of the BNetzA reform), LFP 2 h / 4 h, safety, form `typ="speicher"`.
- **`/kommunen`**: six value streams with a 20 MWp example calculation, the zoning-plan procedure in 6 steps (incl. § 35 privileged sites), criteria catalogue, acceptance and Stadtwerke sections, AT/CH notes, form `typ="kommune"`.
- **`/rechner/kommune`**: § 6 EEG, trade tax (loss carry-forward, 25 % interest add-back, 90 %/100 % allocation to the site municipality) and lease on municipal land. Figures shown per year, over 20 years and over 30 years, with bars per source and a stacked year-by-year chart. Logic: `src/lib/rechner/kommune.js`.
- **`/rechner`** (hub): dark hero, tools grouped by audience, a mini preview per tool in the new `src/components/Rechner/ToolVorschau.js` (using real example calculations), signpost table, FAQ, ItemList schema.
- **New shared files**:
  - `src/components/Rechner/InvestTeile.js` (calculator layout frame, mobile summary bar, hints, legend)
  - `src/components/Carport/AuswahlAnfrage.js` (chip selection in front of `AnfrageFormular`; used on the carport, storage and municipality pages)
  - `src/components/Carport/CarportIllustration.js`
  - `src/components/Speicher/TagesprofilGrafik.js`

### Findings and open points
1. **Returns come out low.** With the original `markt.js` values (capex 530, opex 12), the 10 MWp / 530 €/kWp / 5 ct test case gave an LCOE of about 5.7 ct and a project IRR of about 3–4 %, not the 4–5 ct and 6–9 % in the brief. While I was working, someone else lowered capex to 470, opex to 9 and the grid fixed cost to 35k. The test case now gives LCOE ≈ 5.3 ct and project IRR ≈ 4.3 %; the defaults give LCOE ≈ 4.9 ct and IRR ≈ 4.8 %. I set the self-test bounds to plausibility ranges (LCOE 4.5–6.5 ct, IRR 2–9 %) and did not bend the model to hit the target. The FAQ on the calculator page explains why the default returns are tight.
2. **Hardly any trade tax in the first 20 years.** Depreciation over 20 years plus interest mean tax typically only starts around year 20–25. That is why the municipal calculator also shows 30 years and a "Ø Jahr 21–30" figure. With the current market values, a 10 MWp park pays essentially no trade tax in its first 20 years.
3. **Hydration warning in dev.** Every page logs one hydration mismatch in dev: `RevealObserver` adds `is-visible` before hydration finishes (the diff shows `className="ov-reveal …"` vs `"… is-visible"`). It comes from the shared Reveal system, not from my pages.
4. **No full build run.** I did not run `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-verify next build`, to avoid loading the dev server further. ESLint on my files reports nothing.

### Additions to `markt.js` (append only, each with a source comment)
- **ERLOESE**: `merchantSteigerung: 0.01`, `zuschlagsHistorie` (Federal Network Agency auctions 2025: 4.66 / 4.84 / 5.00 ct), `lcoeIseCt: {4.1, 6.9}` (Fraunhofer ISE 2024)
- **FINANZIERUNG**: `dscrZiel: 1.15`
- **CARPORT**: `laufzeit: 25`, `contractingJahre: 20`, `contractingMarge: 0.1`, `stellplatzM2: 25`
- **KOMMUNE**: `betrachtungJahre: 20`, `afaJahre: 20`, `hinzurechnungZinsen: 0.25`, `hinzurechnungFreibetrag: 200000`, `hebesatzSpanne: {2.0, 6.0}`

### Requests for shared files
- `tools.js`: add a `toolById` export; the hub currently looks tools up itself.
- `RechnerSeite`: an option for a pinned results column / full-width area; I built this myself for now in `InvestTeile.RechnerRahmen`.
- `RevealObserver`: fix the hydration issue in point 3, e.g. by only adding `is-visible` after hydration or with `suppressHydrationWarning`.
- `AnfrageFormular`: accept a preset value for `firma` (e.g. municipality name).

One side note: while screenshotting I accidentally changed the shared `pw/shot.mjs` (wait mode). I restored it straight away; my own variants are `shot2.mjs` and `el.mjs` in the scratchpad.
